He is a pioneer of quantum logic spectroscopy, a technique he co-developed during his postdoc, which allows the spectroscopy of ions that lack suitable transitions for direct laser cooling and detection (such as aluminum and highly charged ions).

name: Mikhail D. Lukin

current_position.title: Joshua and Beth Friedman University Professor of Physics

short_bio: Mikhail Lukin is a Professor of Physics at Harvard University and a co-director of the Harvard Quantum Initiative, working at the interface of quantum optics, quantum information and many-body physics. His group pioneered programmable quantum simulators and quantum processors built from reconfigurable optical-tweezer arrays of rubidium (Rb) atoms excited to Rydberg states, demonstrating 51-atom quantum simulations, hundreds-of-qubit arrays and logical qubits.

He is one of the most cited physicists in quantum simulation, widely recognised for pioneering the use of optical lattices and quantum gas microscopes to realise and probe strongly correlated quantum systems with single-atom precision.

name: Jun Ye

current_position.institution: JILA, University of Colorado Boulder / NIST

short_bio: Jun Ye is a physicist at JILA, a joint institute of NIST and the University of Colorado Boulder, renowned for ultra-precise optical atomic clocks based on strontium atoms and for ultracold molecules. With Deborah Jin, his group created the first high-phase-space-density gas of ground-state polar potassium-rubidium (KRb) molecules and demonstrated ultracold quantum-state-controlled chemistry.

name: Markus Greiner

current_position.title: George Vasmer Leverett Professor of Physics

short_bio: Markus Greiner is the George Vasmer Leverett Professor of Physics at Harvard University, where he has been a faculty member since 2005. He is one of the principal architects of quantum gas microscopy — the technique that enables single-atom imaging and manipulation within optical lattices at the scale of individual lattice sites — and a pioneer of quantum simulation with ultracold atoms.

He co-leads the "Quantum Optics – Atoms" group with Antoine Browaeys, where the team pioneers neutral-atom quantum simulation and computing using arrays of single Rydberg atoms in optical tweezers.

name: Manuel Endres

postdocs.note: HQOC Prize Postdoctoral Fellow, Harvard Quantum Optics Center

short_bio: Manuel Endres is Professor of Physics at the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), where he has led the Endres Lab since 2015 (initially as Visiting Associate, promoted to Assistant Professor in 2016 and Full Professor in 2021). His group develops optical tweezer array platforms for quantum computing, quantum simulation, and precision metrology, with a particular focus on alkaline-earth (strontium) neutral atoms and Rydberg qubit control.

name: Adam M. Kaufman

current_position.title: JILA Fellow and Associate Professor of Physics

short_bio: Adam M. Kaufman is a JILA Fellow, NIST Physicist, and Associate Professor of Physics at the University of Colorado Boulder, where he leads the Kaufman Group at JILA. He joined JILA as an Associate Fellow and Assistant Professor Adjoint in July 2017 and was promoted to JILA Fellow and Associate Professor in March 2022.

name: Jeff D. Thompson

current_position.title: Associate Professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering

short_bio: Jeff D. Thompson is an Associate Professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering at Princeton University, where he joined the faculty as an Assistant Professor in February 2016 and was promoted to Associate Professor in January 2022. He is also affiliated with the Princeton Quantum Initiative.

name: Hannes Bernien
short_bio: Hannes Bernien is a Full Professor of Experimental Physics at the University of Innsbruck and Scientific Director at the Institute for Quantum Optics and Quantum Information (IQOQI) of the Austrian Academy of Sciences, positions he assumed in 2025. Prior to this, he was an Assistant Professor of Molecular Engineering at the University of Chicago's Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering (2019–2025).

name: Mark Saffman
short_bio: Mark Saffman is the Johannes Rydberg Professor of Physics at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, where his group builds neutral-atom quantum computers from optical-tweezer and optical-lattice arrays of cesium (Cs) and rubidium (Rb) atoms, using Rydberg-blockade interactions to implement entangling gates.

name: Dan Stamper-Kurn
short_bio: Dan Stamper-Kurn is a Professor of Physics at the University of California, Berkeley, whose group studies ultracold rubidium (Rb) gases as a platform for quantum many-body physics, precision measurement and cavity optomechanics. His work includes spinor Bose-Einstein condensates, cavity quantum electrodynamics with quantum gases, and optomechanics with atomic ensembles.

name: Christian Groß

current_position.title: W3 Professor of Experimental Many-Particle Quantum Physics

short_bio: Christian Groß is W3 Professor of Experimental Many-Particle Quantum Physics at the University of Tübingen, where he has led the Quantum Many-Body Physics group since September 2019. He is one of the foremost experimentalists in quantum gas microscopy, having co-developed a world-leading platform using ultracold fermionic lithium atoms in optical lattices that enables single-atom and single-spin resolved imaging of strongly correlated quantum many-body systems.

name: Kang-Kuen Ni

current_position.title: Theodore William Richards Professor of Chemistry; Professor of Physics

short_bio: Kang-Kuen Ni is a Professor of Chemistry and Physics at Harvard University, where her group studies ultracold molecules for quantum information and controlled chemistry. Her lab assembled single molecules from individual atoms in optical tweezers (NaCs) and observed bimolecular reactions of ultracold KRb molecules at the state-to-state level.

name: Dolev Bluvstein
short_bio: Dolev Bluvstein is a physicist working on neutral-atom quantum computing with reconfigurable optical-tweezer arrays of rubidium (Rb) atoms and Rydberg interactions. His experiments demonstrated dynamically reconfigurable atom arrays, high-fidelity entanglement, and logical quantum processors with error correction on dozens of logical qubits.

name: Jacob P. Covey
keywords: neutral atom arrays in optical tweezers
short_bio: Jacob Covey is an Assistant Professor of Physics at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, where his group builds optical-tweezer arrays of alkaline-earth(-like) atoms — ytterbium (Yb) and strontium (Sr) — for quantum computing, optical-clock metrology and atom-photon quantum networking.

name: Jonathan D. Pritchard

current_position.title: Professor of Physics (Judith and Harold Rosenberg Chair in Quantum Computing)

short_bio: Jonathan Pritchard is a Professor of Physics at the University of Strathclyde, where his group works on Rydberg atoms in cesium (Cs) and rubidium (Rb) for quantum computing, quantum optics and microwave-to-optical conversion, using optical-tweezer arrays and atomic ensembles.

name: Klaus Mølmer
short_bio: Klaus Mølmer is a theoretical physicist and one of the founding figures of quantum optics and quantum information theory. He is Professor of Physics at the Niels Bohr Institute, University of Copenhagen, where he joined in 2022 after holding a full professorship at Aarhus University from 2000 to 2022.

His work spans long-range-interacting spin systems, Rydberg-atom arrays, ultracold atoms and molecules, quantum optics, and quantum networks and metrology.

name: Ana María Rey

current_position.institution: JILA, University of Colorado Boulder / NIST
current_position.title: JILA Fellow; NIST Fellow; Professor Adjoint of Physics, University of Colorado Boulder

short_bio: Ana Maria Rey is a Fellow of JILA and Professor Adjoint at the University of Colorado Boulder, and a theorist of ultracold matter. Her work connects atomic, molecular and optical physics with condensed-matter and quantum-information science, including spin models with trapped ions and polar molecules, optical-lattice clocks, and the use of entanglement for quantum-enhanced metrology.

name: Hannes Pichler

thesis.title: Atomic quantum simulators - detecting entanglement and designing open many-body dynamics

short_bio: Hannes Pichler is a theoretical physicist and Professor of Theoretical Physics at the University of Innsbruck, where he has held his chair since June 2020. He is also Research Director of the Pichler Group — Quantum Science Theory at the Institute for Quantum Optics and Quantum Information (IQOQI) of the Austrian Academy of Sciences in Innsbruck. He was born in 1986 in Brixen (South Tyrol, Italy).

name: Soonwon Choi

current_position.title: Victor F. Weisskopf Assistant Professor of Physics

short_bio: Soonwon Choi is an Assistant Professor of Physics at MIT and a theorist of quantum many-body dynamics and quantum information. His work addresses thermalization and its breakdown, quantum information scrambling, measurement-induced phenomena, and the dynamics of programmable quantum simulators such as Rydberg-atom arrays.

name: Tommaso Calarco
keywords: Cold Atom Physics and Bose-Einstein Condensates
short_bio: Tommaso Calarco is Director of the Institute for Quantum Control (PGI-8) at Forschungszentrum Jülich, a position he has held since September 2018. He is concurrently Professor of Quantum Information at the University of Cologne and the University of Bologna. He is one of Europe's foremost figures in quantum technologies policy and quantum optimal control theory.

name: Andrew J. Daley
keywords: Cold Atom Physics and Bose-Einstein Condensates
short_bio: Andrew J. Daley is Professor of Quantum Physics in the Atomic and Laser Physics sub-department at the University of Oxford, and Tutorial Fellow in Physics at Keble College. His research spans the boundary between quantum optics, many-body physics, and quantum technologies, focusing on non-equilibrium dynamics of ultracold quantum gases, open quantum systems, and tensor-network numerical methods.

He previously held a Niels Bohr Professorship at Aarhus University (2017–2023) funded by the Danish National Research Foundation, and was a Group Leader at the Max Planck Institute for the Physics of Complex Systems in Dresden (2008–2017).

name: Hans Peter Büchler

short_bio: Hans Peter Büchler is Professor of Theoretical Physics at the Institute for Theoretical Physics III (ITP3) at the University of Stuttgart, where he has held the chair since 2007. He holds the degree Dr. sc. nat. (Doctor of Natural Sciences) from ETH Zürich (2003), where he worked under Gianni Blatter on phase transitions in quantum condensed matter. He then carried out postdoctoral research from 2004 to 2007 with Peter Zoller at the University of Innsbruck, which shaped his focus on cold-atom quantum simulation and Rydberg physics.

name: Igor Lesanovsky

keywords: Cold Atom Physics and Bose-Einstein Condensates
short_bio: Igor Lesanovsky is a Professor of Physics at the University of Tübingen (and the University of Nottingham), and a theorist of open quantum many-body systems. His work focuses on the non-equilibrium and dissipative dynamics of strongly interacting Rydberg gases, quantum kinetically constrained models, and emergent collective phenomena.

name: Markus Müller

postdocs.note: Theoretical Physics Department

short_bio: Markus Müller is a Professor of Physics at RWTH Aachen University and Forschungszentrum Jülich, and a theorist of quantum error correction and fault-tolerant quantum computing. His work develops topological and color codes, fault-tolerant logical operations, and co-design with trapped-ion and Rydberg-atom hardware, as well as the theory of open and dissipative quantum systems.

name: Dieter Jaksch

current_position.title: Professor of Physics (Theory of Many-Body Quantum Optical Systems)

keywords: Cold Atom Physics and Bose-Einstein Condensates
short_bio: Dieter Jaksch is a theoretical physicist and Professor for Theory of Many-Body Quantum Optical Systems at the Institute for Quantum Physics, Universität Hamburg, which he joined in the winter semester of 2021/22. He was previously Professor of Physics at the University of Oxford (2010–2021), where he had been a faculty member since 2003.

short_bio: Guido Pupillo is a Distinguished Professor at the Université de Strasbourg, where he directs the European Center for Quantum Sciences (CESQ) and the Quantum Physics Laboratory at ISIS. He is a leading theorist in the physics of Rydberg-dressed atoms and strongly correlated quantum many-body systems.

name: Ronald Hanson

current_position.title: Distinguished Professor in Quantum Computing and Quantum Internet

short_bio: Ronald Hanson is a physicist at Delft University of Technology (QuTech) who uses nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centres in diamond as spin qubits for quantum networks. His group performed the first loophole-free Bell test and demonstrated entanglement, teleportation and entanglement distillation between remote NV registers — key steps toward a quantum internet.

name: Fedor Jelezko

current_position.title: Professor (W3), Director of the Institute for Quantum Optics

short_bio: Fedor Jelezko is a physicist at the University of Ulm who pioneered the optical readout and coherent control of single nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centres in diamond. His group develops NV-based quantum sensing, including nanoscale magnetic resonance and single-molecule NMR.

name: Jörg Wrachtrup

current_position.title: Professor of Physics, Director of the 3rd Physical Institute

short_bio: Jörg Wrachtrup is a physicist at the University of Stuttgart and a founder of single-spin quantum science with nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centres in diamond. His group develops NV-based quantum sensing and imaging, nanoscale NMR, and defect-based quantum information.

name: David D. Awschalom

current_position.title: Liew Family Professor in Molecular Engineering

short_bio: David Awschalom is a physicist at the University of Chicago and Argonne National Laboratory and a leader in spintronics and quantum information with defects in wide-bandgap crystals. His group studies nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centres in diamond and divacancies in silicon carbide for quantum sensing, communication and computing, and he directs a national quantum-networking effort.

name: Nathalie P. de Leon

current_position.title: Associate Professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering

keywords: color centers in wide bandgap materials
short_bio: Nathalie de Leon is a physicist at Princeton University working on solid-state qubits and their materials. Her group develops nitrogen-vacancy (NV) and group-IV (tin-vacancy, SnV) colour centres in diamond for quantum networks and sensing, and investigates the materials limits of superconducting-qubit coherence.

name: Ania C. Bleszynski Jayich

current_position.title: Bruker Endowed Chair in Science and Engineering, Professor of Physics

short_bio: Ania Bleszynski Jayich is a physicist at the University of California, Santa Barbara who uses nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centres in diamond for nanoscale quantum sensing, including scanning NV magnetometry of condensed-matter systems.

name: Lee C. Bassett

current_position.title: Associate Professor of Electrical and Systems Engineering

short_bio: Lee Bassett is a physicist at the University of Pennsylvania working on quantum defects. His group studies nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centres in diamond and emerging colour centres, including in hexagonal boron nitride, for quantum sensing and information.

name: Marcus W. Doherty
keywords: NV center theory and electronic structure
short_bio: Marcus Doherty is a theoretical physicist (Australian National University) known for the theory of the nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centre in diamond, which underpins NV-based quantum sensing and information.

name: Shimon Kolkowitz

current_position.title: Associate Professor and Herst Chair in Physics

short_bio: Shimon Kolkowitz is a physicist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison (previously UC Berkeley) working on quantum sensing with nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centres in diamond and on optical-lattice atomic clocks for precision measurement.

name: Liang Jiang

postdocs.note: Sherman Fairchild Postdoctoral Fellow

short_bio: Liang Jiang is a theoretical physicist at the University of Chicago working on quantum information science across platforms — bosonic quantum error correction, quantum networks and microwave-optical transduction, and quantum sensing with solid-state and superconducting systems.

name: Dirk Englund

current_position.title: Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science

short_bio: Dirk Englund is a physicist at MIT working on quantum photonics and solid-state qubits. His group develops nitrogen-vacancy and group-IV (tin-vacancy, SnV) colour centres in diamond, integrated photonics and quantum networks.

name: Tim H. Taminiau

education.institution: ICFO – The Institute of Photonic Sciences

short_bio: Tim Taminiau is a physicist at Delft University of Technology (QuTech) who builds multi-qubit quantum processors from a nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centre and the surrounding nuclear spins in diamond, demonstrating ten-plus-qubit registers and quantum error correction.

name: Patrick Maletinsky
short_bio: Patrick Maletinsky is a physicist at the University of Basel who develops scanning nitrogen-vacancy (NV) magnetometry, using single NV centres in diamond tips to image magnetic textures at the nanoscale.

name: Gregory D. Fuchs

current_position.title: James R. Meehl Professor of Applied and Engineering Physics

short_bio: Gregory Fuchs is a physicist at Cornell University working with nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centres in diamond, including spin-mechanical and spin-magnon coupling and high-speed coherent spin control.

name: Christian L. Degen
short_bio: Christian Degen is a physicist at ETH Zurich who develops nanoscale magnetic resonance imaging and scanning magnetometry using nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centres in diamond.

name: Sophia E. Economou

current_position.title: Professor and T. Marshall Hahn Chair in Physics

short_bio: Sophia Economou is a theoretical physicist at Virginia Tech working on solid-state and photonic quantum information — spin qubits and colour centres, the deterministic generation of photonic graph states and all-photonic quantum repeaters, and quantum algorithms.

name: Nir Bar-Gill

postdocs.note: Studied many-body spin physics and coherence properties of NV centres in diamond.

short_bio: Prof. Nir Bar-Gill is a Full Professor jointly appointed in the Racah Institute of Physics and the Department of Applied Physics at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. He heads the Quantum Information, Simulation and Sensing (QISS) lab.

name: Lilian Childress
short_bio: Lilian Childress is a physicist at McGill University working on nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centres in diamond for quantum networks, developing spin-photon entanglement and NV-based quantum repeaters.

name: M. V. Gurudev Dutt
short_bio: M. V. Gurudev Dutt is a physicist at the University of Pittsburgh who uses nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centres in diamond as quantum registers, coupling a single electronic spin to nearby nuclear spins for quantum information and high-dynamic-range magnetometry.

short_bio: Jiangfeng Du (born June 1969, Wuxi, Jiangsu) is a Chinese physicist and academician of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (elected 2015) who built one of the world's leading groups in spin-based quantum information and precision measurement using nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond.

short_bio: Christoph Becher is a physicist at Saarland University who develops group-IV colour centres in diamond — silicon-vacancy (SiV) and tin-vacancy (SnV) — as spin-photon interfaces for quantum networks, together with quantum frequency conversion.

short_bio: Cristian Bonato is a physicist at Heriot-Watt University working on nitrogen-vacancy (NV) and other colour centres, with a focus on real-time adaptive measurement and machine-learning-enhanced quantum sensing.

name: Igor Aharonovich
short_bio: Igor Aharonovich is a physicist at the University of Technology Sydney who develops quantum emitters and colour centres in wide-bandgap materials — notably hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) and diamond — and integrated quantum nanophotonics.

name: Machiel Blok

current_position.title: Assistant Professor of Physics and Astronomy

short_bio: Machiel Blok is Assistant Professor of Physics and Astronomy at the University of Rochester, where he leads the Blok Lab. He completed his PhD at Delft University of Technology under Ronald Hanson, working on quantum measurement and real-time feedback with NV center spin registers in diamond. Following a postdoc in Irfan Siddiqi's group at UC Berkeley and Lawrence Berkeley National Lab (2015–2019), he joined Rochester in 2020. His current research focuses on qudit quantum computing and quantum simulation with superconducting transmon circuits, pioneering the use of higher-dimensional (beyond qubit) encodings to improve quantum processor performance and error resilience.

name: Wolfgang Pfaff
short_bio: Wolfgang Pfaff is an experimental physicist working on superconducting quantum circuits, with a focus on modular quantum processors and quantum networking. His work uses transmon qubits coupled to three-dimensional microwave cavities to build error-correctable bosonic memories and to transfer quantum states between separated modules over microwave links.

name: John M. Martinis
short_bio: John M. Martinis is an experimental physicist and a leading figure in superconducting quantum computing. He earned his BS (1980) and PhD (1987) in physics at the University of California, Berkeley under John Clarke, where his thesis work on macroscopic quantum tunnelling and energy-level quantisation in Josephson junctions later earned him the 2025 Nobel Prize in Physics, shared with Clarke and Michel Devoret.

He co-founded circuit quantum electrodynamics (cQED), co-invented the transmon qubit, and has led experimental demonstrations of quantum algorithms and error correction in superconducting integrated circuits.

short_bio: Michel Devoret is a founding figure of superconducting quantum circuits. His work established the quantum behavior of Josephson-junction circuits and includes the invention of the transmon qubit, quantum-limited Josephson parametric amplifiers (the Josephson parametric converter), and the use of microwave cavities and 'cat' states for hardware-efficient quantum error correction.

short_bio: Steven Girvin is a theoretical physicist at Yale University and a principal architect of circuit quantum electrodynamics (circuit QED) — the theory describing superconducting qubits strongly coupled to microwave photons. His work underpins dispersive qubit readout and the field of bosonic quantum error correction, including cat codes and Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) codes that encode logical qubits in microwave cavity modes.

short_bio: Andrew Houck is an experimental physicist at Princeton University working on superconducting circuit QED. His group studies transmon qubits, ultra-low-loss materials and coherence, and lattices of superconducting microwave resonators and qubits — including hyperbolic and other engineered lattices — as analog quantum simulators of photonic many-body physics.

short_bio: David Schuster is the Joan Reinhart Professor of Applied Physics at Stanford University, where his group develops superconducting quantum circuits for quantum computing, simulation, and hybrid quantum systems. He previously held a faculty position at the University of Chicago (c. 2012–2022). He completed his PhD and postdoc in the Schoelkopf Lab at Yale, where he was first author on the landmark 2007 Nature paper resolving individual photon number states in a superconducting circuit. His Stanford group pursues fluxonium-based high-fidelity gates, cavity-array quantum simulation, millimeter-wave to optical transduction via cold atoms, electron-on-helium qubits, and quantum-enhanced dark matter detection.

short_bio: Irfan Siddiqi is an experimental physicist at the University of California, Berkeley and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, where he leads the Advanced Quantum Testbed. His group pioneered quantum-limited Josephson parametric amplifiers and the continuous monitoring and feedback control of superconducting transmon qubits, tracking individual quantum trajectories, and builds multi-qubit superconducting processors.

short_bio: Andrew Cleland is an experimental physicist at the University of Chicago and Argonne National Laboratory. With John Martinis he built the first 'quantum machine' — a mechanical resonator in its quantum ground state coupled to a superconducting phase qubit. His group works on circuit quantum acoustodynamics, using surface- and bulk-acoustic-wave phonons as quantum resources, and on modular quantum networking between superconducting qubits via microwave communication channels.

short_bio: Konrad Lehnert is an experimental physicist at JILA and the University of Colorado Boulder and NIST. His group develops quantum-limited microwave measurement and amplification, superconducting electromechanics, and quantum transducers that convert quantum information between microwave (superconducting-qubit) and optical frequencies for quantum networking.

short_bio: Göran Wendin is a theoretical physicist at Chalmers University of Technology and an early advocate and theorist of superconducting quantum computing in Europe. His work spans the theory of Josephson-junction qubits, decoherence, and the roadmaps and reviews that helped shape the European superconducting-qubit research agenda.

short_bio: Per Delsing is an experimental physicist at Chalmers University of Technology working on superconducting circuits and quantum acoustics. His group demonstrated a single artificial atom coupled to propagating microwave photons, observed the dynamical Casimir effect with a superconducting circuit, and pioneered quantum acoustics with surface-acoustic-wave (SAW) phonons coupled to transmon qubits.

short_bio: Andreas Wallraff is an experimental physicist at ETH Zurich who, with the Yale group, performed the first experiments demonstrating strong coupling of a single superconducting qubit to a microwave photon in a resonator — a foundational result of circuit QED. His group works on transmon-based quantum processors, deterministic microwave quantum teleportation, real-time quantum error correction with the surface code, and cryogenic microwave links between distributed processors.

short_bio: Jens Koch is a theoretical physicist at Northwestern University and a co-inventor of the transmon qubit, the most widely used superconducting qubit design. His work develops the theory of superconducting circuits — including fluxonium and other protected qubits, circuit quantization, and the widely used scQubits software — and circuit-QED lattices for quantum simulation.

His group works on superconducting qubits, cavity and crystal optomechanics, and quantum acoustics, using phononic and photonic crystals and engineered acoustic resonators to interface superconducting circuits with mechanical and optical degrees of freedom for quantum information and networking.

name: Yasunobu Nakamura
short_bio: Yasunobu Nakamura is an experimental physicist at the University of Tokyo and the director of the RIKEN Center for Quantum Computing. In 1999 he demonstrated the first coherent control of a superconducting qubit (a Cooper-pair-box charge qubit), launching the field of superconducting quantum computing. His work spans microwave quantum optics, quantum acoustics, hybrid quantum systems, and large-scale superconducting quantum processors.

name: Leonardo DiCarlo
short_bio: Leonardo DiCarlo is an experimental physicist at TU Delft and QuTech. His group builds multi-transmon quantum processors, demonstrating early two-qubit quantum algorithms, fast feedback and reset, and experimental quantum error correction with repetition and surface codes.

short_bio: Alexandre Blais is Full Professor (Professeur titulaire) of Physics at Université de Sherbrooke and Scientific Director of the Institut quantique. He is the co-inventor of circuit quantum electrodynamics (circuit QED), the theoretical architecture — coupling superconducting qubits to microwave resonators — that underpins superconducting quantum processors at Google, IBM, and Amazon. He obtained his PhD at Sherbrooke (2002), did a postdoc with Girvin and Schoelkopf at Yale (2003–2005), then returned to Sherbrooke as faculty. He is a CIFAR Fellow (Quantum Information Science), Fellow of the American Physical Society, Member of the Royal Society of Canada, and has received the NSERC Steacie Fellowship (2010), Herzberg Medal (2011), Brockhouse Medal (2020), Rutherford Memorial Medal (2018), and Guggenheim Fellowship (2021).

His work develops Josephson parametric amplifiers and nonreciprocal (directional, isolator-free) superconducting microwave devices that enable high-fidelity readout of superconducting qubits.

His group develops fluxonium qubits and high-kinetic-inductance superinductors made from granular aluminum, pursuing low-loss materials, long coherence, and intrinsically protected qubit designs.

short_bio: John Clarke is an experimental physicist at the University of California, Berkeley and a pioneer of superconducting quantum interference devices (SQUIDs) and ultra-sensitive magnetometry. His experiments on macroscopic quantum tunneling and energy-level quantization in current-biased Josephson junctions provided foundational evidence that Josephson circuits behave quantum-mechanically — the basis for superconducting qubits.

His group characterizes and mitigates noise and decoherence, develops high-fidelity single- and two-qubit gates, and builds scalable superconducting quantum processors.

Her group couples superconducting transmon qubits to bulk-acoustic-wave (phonon) resonators, creating and controlling non-classical mechanical states for quantum memory, transduction and tests of macroscopic quantum mechanics.

His group couples superconducting microwave resonators to semiconductor quantum-dot spin and Andreev qubits, using superconducting circuits as a quantum bus to mediate long-range interactions between disparate qubit platforms.

short_bio: Ian Alexander Walmsley CBE FRS is Director of the Oxford Quantum Institute and Professor of Physics at the University of Oxford (from October 2025). He is a world-leading expert in ultrafast and quantum optics, known for inventing the SPIDER (Spectral Phase Interferometry for Direct Electric-field Reconstruction) technique for ultrashort-pulse characterisation, and for foundational contributions to photonic quantum computing, quantum memories, and photon-pair generation. He received his BSc from Imperial College London and his PhD (1986) from the Institute of Optics, University of Rochester, under Michael G. Raymer, before joining the Rochester faculty (1988–2001, including Director of the Institute 2000–2001). He then moved to Oxford as Hooke Professor of Experimental Physics and Pro-Vice-Chancellor for Research, before serving as Provost and Chair of Experimental Physics at Imperial College London (2018–2025). He is a co-founder of ORCA Computing (2019) and was Director of the Networked Quantum Information Technologies (NQIT) Hub. He was elected Fellow of the Royal Society in 2012 and awarded the Rumford Medal in 2018.

name: Nicolas Gisin
short_bio: Nicolas Gisin (born 1952) is Professor Emeritus of Physics at the University of Geneva, where he led the Quantum Information and Communication (QIC) group in the Department of Applied Physics for more than two decades. He is one of the founding figures of experimental quantum cryptography and long-distance quantum communication. In 1993 he demonstrated quantum key distribution in optical fiber, and in 1997 his group performed the first Bell inequality violation test with photons more than 10 km apart over deployed telecom fiber beneath Lake Geneva. In 2003 the group achieved the first long-distance teleportation of qubits at telecommunication wavelengths. He co-founded ID Quantique in 2001, one of the world's first commercial quantum cryptography companies. His 2002 Reviews of Modern Physics article on quantum cryptography (with Ribordy, Tittel, and Zbinden) has accumulated more than 12,000 citations and remains the standard reference in the field. Despite emeritus status he remains research-active, publishing in 2024 on Bell inequalities and foundational quantum mechanics, and was awarded the Micius Quantum Prize in 2023 and an honorary doctorate from the University of York in 2025.

short_bio: Anthony Laing is Professor of Physics and Co-Director of QET Labs (Quantum Engineering Technology Labs) at the University of Bristol. He is a leading experimentalist in integrated photonic quantum computing and simulation. His group pioneers reconfigurable waveguide chips that implement quantum walks, boson sampling, and molecular vibrational simulations — using programmable silica-on-silicon and silicon photonic circuits to process quantum information with single photons. He invented the Reference Frame Independent Quantum Key Distribution (RFI-QKD) protocol (2010, patented with Nokia) and contributed to landmark demonstrations including the first fully reconfigurable entanglement chip (Nature Photonics 2012), the universal linear optics processor (Science 2015), and photonic molecular dynamics simulation (Nature 2018). In 2016 he was appointed Lecturer in Physics and awarded a 5-year EPSRC Quantum Technologies Fellowship; he was later promoted to full Professor. He obtained both his MSc and PhD from the University of Bristol, working in Jeremy O'Brien's Centre for Quantum Photonics. In 2020 he co-founded Duality Quantum Photonics (with Alberto Politi as CTO), a Bristol spin-out developing scalable integrated photonic quantum hardware, and serves as its CEO.

short_bio: Ulrik Lund Andersen (born 1972) is Professor of Physics at the Technical University of Denmark (DTU) and Director of bigQ — the Center for Macroscopic Quantum States — where he heads the Quantum Information group. He is one of the leading figures in continuous-variable (CV) quantum information, pioneering experimental and theoretical work on squeezed light, photonic cluster states, CV quantum key distribution, hybrid discrete-CV protocols, and bosonic error correction with the Gottesman–Kitaev–Preskill (GKP) code.
